title: Against Notes 8, 2026
author: Kane, Dylan
source: Five Twelve Thirteen (Substack), via Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #122 roundup, September
summary: Dylan Kane, cited in Craig Barton's roundup, separates two things usually bundled together in classroom notetaking policy: the act of writing during a lesson, which he considers genuinely valuable for learning, and the expectation that students will later reference those same notes, which he argues is not supported and carries a real cost. His central frame is opportunity cost — the classroom time and student effort spent maintaining reference-quality notes could instead go toward more active study methods that the cognitive-science literature rates more highly, such as summarizing in one's own words and self-testing. He cites a specific cognitive-science finding that when students refer back to their own notes, they systematically overestimate how much they have actually learned, which undercuts notes' apparent value as a study aid even when students believe it is working. Kane also challenges the common justification that notetaking itself is a transferable skill worth teaching for its own sake, arguing instead that most classroom notetaking routines function primarily as a compliance exercise rather than a genuine learning strategy, and that redirecting that same time toward active summarizing and independent practice would teach students more.
points: Kane separates the act of writing during a lesson (which he considers valuable) from the expectation that students will later reference those notes (which he argues is not supported by evidence).
His central argument is one of opportunity cost: time spent making notes reference-worthy could instead go toward more active study methods that the literature rates more highly.
He cites a specific cognitive finding that when students refer back to their own notes, they overestimate how much they have actually learned.

He challenges the assumption that notetaking is itself a valuable transferable skill, arguing most classroom notetaking routines function as compliance exercises rather than genuine learning strategies.
His alternative is directing that time toward active techniques such as summarizing ideas in one's own words and self-testing, which he argues produce more actual learning.
quotes: I don't stress about whether the things that are written down are useful for students to reference in the future.
The argument I'm making here is fundamentally about opportunity cost.
Looking back at notes is consistently inferior to other, more active ways of studying.
When students refer back to their notes, they overestimate how much they have learned.
A student who has practice summarizing ideas in their own words and being an active participant in their learning is going to learn a lot more.
